event: Half six, Wednesday: Bea bangs on your door; you groan, and go, legs still stiff from yesterday.
Bea makes you run slow this time; you last ten minutes before your lungs give, double yesterday.
Out on the mere a capped head moves through the grey water; Shiv lifts an arm and waves.
You wave back, and only go a little red; Bea notices and grins the whole way home.
Hot water again, and you stand under it until a fist on the door says it's someone else's turn.
Ten o'clock: Sigils, in the Drawing Room, long rows of slanted desks under skylights.
Ink pots, steel nibs, thick cream paper; the sigils tutor, a small brisk woman, teaches in ink.
Group F sits among two other groups; you take the desk beside Lin, who looks quietly pleased.
Kit takes the desk in front of you, back straight, and keeps her eyes on her paper.
Your first nib blots; your second scratches through the paper; Lin slides you a softer nib.
She shows you how to hold the pen loose, and load less ink; her fingers move yours once.
On paper, slow, with nobody watching, your glim sigil comes out clean: stroke, loop, hook in.
The tutor walks the rows and stops at Lin's desk; she holds Lin's page up for the whole room.
"This," she says, "is a sigil." Lin goes scarlet to the ears and stares at her inkwell.
After, you tell Lin under your breath that the tutor's right; Lin hides her smile in her sleeve.
Leaving the Drawing Room, Kit falls into step beside you in the corridor, eyes ahead.
"Whatever you think you saw last night," she says, low and clipped.
You say you saw the best glims in the year, and that it's hers, and you've told nobody.
Kit stops walking; she looks at you properly for the first time since the dinner.
"Thank you," she says, stiffly, as if the word costs her.
"Stop thanking me," you say; Kit's mouth twitches, and then she laughs, once, surprised.
She walks off fast, ears pink; you stand in the corridor grinning at the stone floor.
Lunch, quick; Bea announces the afternoon is free by old custom and everyone walks to the village.
Bea collects you, and you collect Lin from the floor below; Lin says yes before Bea finishes.
The shore path is a mile of shingle and bracken, the fells bright, the wind cold off the mere.
Shiv catches you up halfway, parka open, hair damp, and walks with you as if invited.
Hollowmere village: one slate-roofed street along the shore, a pub, a shop, a tearoom by a jetty.
The pub is the Drowned Bell, low-beamed; Shiv says the jukebox is older than any of you.
The shop sells bread, stamps, cheap charms, ink and paper; Lin buys a bottle of black ink.
In the charity shop Bea dresses you like a doll: an old fisherman's jumper, a wool hat.
Lin finds a battered book of sigils from the fifties and holds it like treasure.
Bea pays for your jumper and waves it off: you can buy the scones next week.
Kit stops walking and turns to you, and looks at you straight on, in daylight, for a long moment.
You split one with Bea, cream and jam; Shiv eats two; Lin eats half of hers very slowly.
Amara sweeps past your table with second-years, touches your shoulder, says, "Freckles."
You go red; Shiv laughs so hard she has to put her head on the table.
Walking back at dusk, Shiv takes you out onto the slab of rock where she swims every dawn.
She dares you to put your feet in; you do; the cold is so total you shriek and she cackles.
"Come in with me some morning," Shiv says, easy; you say maybe, and mean it more than you expected.
Bea links her arm through yours on the last stretch, your new jumper scratchy and warm.
Evening, the Thornfield kitchen: Lin comes up with her new ink and the old sigil book.
You practise the glim with Lin beside you, curling the hook in, slow, the way she drew it.
The spark comes, and this time it lifts an inch off your palm and lasts two heartbeats.
Lin makes a small pleased sound; you grab her inky hand without thinking, and she lets you.
She takes her hand back gently after a moment, pink, and says goodnight.
Alone in room 14 you take out the empty phone and type Alan's old number from memory.
You stare at it a long time, thumb over the button, then delete it, unsent.
Your head aches from the practice; you go down the corridor and knock on room 1.
Yusra opens the door in a soft jumper, reading glasses on, a healing textbook open behind her.
Her room is neat as a ward: books squared, a kettle, a small bowl of lemons by the window.
She sits you on her desk chair, and takes your wrist to feel your pulse, a healer's habit.
She tells you it's a lighter headache than yesterday's; you're overreaching less already.
She gives you water and two paracetamol, and asks how the day was, and actually listens.
You tell her about the scones and the jumper and the rock; you leave Kit out.
She says Doyle will have you swimming in the mere by term's end, and she'll pretend not to know.
At the door her hand rests on your shoulder a moment: "Sleep, Ashby." You do, almost at once.
A day at Hollowmere ends.
